title: 1  Introduction
text:
The stelfi package fits Hawkes and log-Gaussian Cox Point Process models, with extensions, using Template Model Builder (Kristensen et al. (2016)).
Overview
A Hawkes process is a self-exciting temporal point process where the occurrence of an event immediately increases the chance of another (see Hawkes (1971)). stelfi also offers functionality to fit self-inhibiting process and a non-homogeneous background rate.
A log-Gaussian Cox process is a Poisson point process where the log-intensity is given by a Gaussian random field. stelfi also offers functionality to extend this to a joint likelihood formulation fitting a marked log-Gaussian Cox model.
In addition, the stelfi offers functionality to fit self-exciting spatiotemporal point processes. Models are fitted via maximum likelihood using ‘TMB’ (Template Model Builder) (Kristensen et al. (2016)). Where included 1) random fields are assumed to be Gaussian and are integrated over using the Laplace approximation and 2) a stochastic partial differential equation model, introduced by Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011), is defined for the field(s).




Hawkes, AG. 1971. “Spectra of Some Self-Exciting and Mutually Exciting Point Processes.” Biometrika.


Kristensen, Kasper, Anders Nielsen, Casper W. Berg, Hans Skaug, and Bradley M. Bell. 2016. “TMB: Automatic Differentiation and Laplace Approximation.” Journal of Statistical Software. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v070.i05.

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes
text:
2.1 Simulating from a univariate Hawkes model
A univariate Hawkes process (Hawkes (1971)) is defined to be a self-exciting temporal point process where the conditional intensity function is given by
\[\lambda(t) = \mu(t) + \Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t}\nu(t-\tau_i).\]
Here \(\mu(t)\) is the background rate of the process and \(\Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t}\nu(t-\tau_i)\) is some historic temporal dependence (i.e., for times \(\tau_i < t\), $ i = 1, …, T$). The classic homogeneous formulation uses an exponential decay kernal:
\[\lambda(t) = \mu + \alpha \Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t}\text{exp}(-\beta * (t-\tau_i)). \tag{2.1}\]
Here the parameter \(\alpha\) is the increase in intensity immediately after the occurrence of an event, and \(\beta > 0\) controls the exponential decay of the intensity if no event has occurred. To avoid the conditional intensity heading off to infinity \(\beta > \alpha\). See (hawkesnll?) for the negative log-likelihood written in R syntax.
Plotted below is the conditional intensity (\(\lambda(t), t \in [0,T]\)) of a Hawkes process with \(\mu = 0.1\), \(\alpha = 1\), and \(\beta = 1.5\). Observed events (n = 13) are shown by the vertical dashes along the x-axis. The intensity increases immediately after an event occurs and decays exponentially over time if no event is observed for some period.
The function sim_hawkes() offers two simulation methods for simulating a realisation of a univariate Hawkes process. The default, with method = 1, uses the same method as algorithm 2 in Ogata (1981), simulating until a given time horizon (set by argument n).
sim <- sim_hawkes(mu = 0.5, alpha = 1, beta = 1.5, n = 40, plot = TRUE)
The second option, setting method = 2, uses an accept/reject framework and the argument n specifies the number of points to simulate (default n = 100).
sim <- sim_hawkes(mu = 0.5, alpha = 1, beta = 1.5, plot = TRUE, method = 2)

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes
text:
2.2 Fitting a univariate Hawkes model

require(stelfi)

To fit a univariate Hawkes model in stelfi use the function fit_hawkes() with the following required arguments

times - a vector of numeric occurrence times, and
parameters - a vector of named starting values for \(\mu\) (mu), \(\alpha\) (alpha), and \(\beta\) (beta).

The function get_coefs() can then be called on the fitted model object to return the estimated parameter values.

2.2.1 A simulated example
Simulating a realisation of a univariate Hawkes process (see Section 2.1 for more details) with \(\mu = 1.3\), \(\alpha = 0.4\), and \(\beta = 1.5\) (over \(t \in [0, 500]\)).

times <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500)


## starting values
sv <- c(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5)
## using stelfi
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
stelfi <- get_coefs(fit)

2.2.2 An applied example
A NIWA scientist found a working USB in the scat of a leopard seal, they then tweeted about it in the hopes of finding its owner1. The dates and times of these tweets and retweets are available in stelfi as retweets_niwa.

data(retweets_niwa)

The dates/times need to be numeric and sorted in ascending order (starting a time \(t = 0\)). Note too that there can be no simultaneous events.

## numeric time stamps
times <- unique(sort(as.numeric(difftime(retweets_niwa ,min(retweets_niwa),units = "mins"))))

The histogram below shows the observed counts (4772) of unique retweet times from the original tweet (\(t=0\)) to the time (just over two days later) that the owner of the USB came forward, t = 3143 mins.









To fit the model chose some starting values for the parameters and supply these along with the numeric times to the function fit_hawkes().

sv <- c(mu = 9, alpha = 3, beta = 10)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv) 


## print out estimated parameters
pars <- get_coefs(fit)
pars

        Estimate  Std. Error
mu    0.06328099 0.017783908
alpha 0.07596531 0.007777899
beta  0.07911346 0.008109789


From the estimated coefficients above

the expected (estimated) background rate of sightings (i.e., independent sightings) is \(\hat{\mu}T =\) 0.063 \(\times\) 3143.02 \(=\) 198.89, which indicates that ~199 retweets (from the 4772) were principal retweets and that the remaining were due to self-excitement;
the expected number of retweets “triggered” by any one retweet is estimated as \(\frac{\hat{\alpha}}{\hat{\beta}}\) = 0.96 (note the maximum this can possibly be is 1);
the expected number of descendants per retweet is estimated as \(\frac{\hat{\beta}}{\hat{\beta} - \hat{\alpha}}\) = 25.13;
the rate of decay for the self-excitement is estimated as \(\frac{1}{\hat{\beta}}\) = 12.64, indicating that after ~13 minutes a retweet is likely unrelated2 to the previous retweet.

The show_hawkes() function can be called on the fitted model object to plot the estimated conditional intensity and the data, top and bottom panels below respectively.

show_hawkes(fit)

section: 2.3 Goodness-of-fit for a univariate Hawkes process
text:
2.3 Goodness-of-fit for a univariate Hawkes process
The compensator, \(\Lambda(\tilde{t})\), of any inhomogeneous Poisson process gives the expected number of events in some defined interval \([0, \tilde{t}]\) is given by
\[\Lambda(\tilde{t}) = \int_0^{\tilde{t}} \lambda(t) dt.\]
The random change theorem (Daley, Vere-Jones, et al. (2003)) states that if a set of events \([\tau_1, ..., \tau_n]\) is a realisation from a inhomogeneous Poisson process then \([\Lambda(\tau_1), ..., \Lambda(\tau_n)]\) is a realisation of a homogeneous Poisson process with unit rate. Letting \(\delta \Lambda_{i} = \Lambda(\tau_i) - \Lambda(\tau_{i-1})\) for \(i = 2, ..., N\) and \(\delta \Lambda_{1} = \Lambda(\tau_1)\), under the theorem above \(\delta \Lambda_{i} \sim \text{Exp}(1)\). Using this result a typical goodness-of-fit test is a Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test (see Daley, Vere-Jones, et al. (2003) for more details) where the KS statistic is a measure of the distance between the empirical distribution of all \(\delta \Lambda_{i}\) and the CDF of a \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution.
The compensator differences can be extracted from a fitted model using the compensator_differences() function, and a KS test can be carried out manually:

times <- sim_hawkes(mu = 1.3, alpha = 0.4, beta = 1.5, n = 500)
sv <- c(mu = 2, alpha = 1, beta = 5)
fit <- fit_hawkes(times = times, parameters = sv)
compensator <- compensator_differences(fit)
stats::ks.test(compensator, "pexp")


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  compensator
D = 0.013855, p-value = 0.9958
alternative hypothesis: two-sided


This gives no evidence against the compensator values coming from a \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distribution.
Another goodness-of-fit test is the Box-Ljung (or Ljung–Box) test, which tests for autocorrelation between the consecutive compensator values (i.e., independence/stationarity).

stats::Box.test(compensator, type = "Ljung")


    Box-Ljung test

data:  compensator
X-squared = 0.66599, df = 1, p-value = 0.4145


This gives no evidence against the consecutive compensator values being independently distributed.
Alternatively, both tests and some diagnostic plots are returned by calling the show_hawkes_GOF() function. The four panels an be interpreted as follows

top left, plots the compensator values against the observed times, which under a well fitting model should align;
top right, a transformed QQ plot, the observed quantities should align with the theoretical quantiles under a well fitting model;
bottom left, the compensator differences, which under the model are assumed to be \(\text{Exp}(1)\) distributed;
bottom right, consecutive compensator differences, which should show no obvious pattern (no autocorrelation evident) under a well fitting model.


show_hawkes_GOF(fit)


    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  interarrivals
D = 0.013855, p-value = 0.9958
alternative hypothesis: two-sided


    Box-Ljung test

data:  interarrivals
X-squared = 0.66599, df = 1, p-value = 0.4145

title: 2  Univariate Hawkes
text:
2.4 Fitting an inhomogenous Hawkes model
A univariate inhomogenous Hawkes process has \(\mu = \mu(t)\) in Equation 2.1 (i.e., the baseline is time varying, rather than being constant).
Below we simulate data from a Hawkes process with \(\mu(t) = [A + B*\text{sin}(\frac{2 \pi t}{365.25})]\) (with \(A = 1\) and \(B = 0.5\)) to represent a yearly cycle and self-exciting parameters \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\beta = 2\) using hawkesbow (Cheysson (2021)).

mut <- function(t) {
 1 + 0.5*sin((2*pi*t)/365.25)
}


set.seed(1)
times <- hawkesbow::hawkes(1000, fun = mut,
 M = 1.5, repr = 0.5, family = "exp", rate = 2)$p

To fit this model in stelfi the function \(\mu(t)\) (background) and its integral \(\int_0^t \mu(y) dy\) (background_integral) are supplied by the user. To ensure \(\mu(t) > 0\) below \(\mu(t)\) is written as a function of \(x\) and \(y\), where \(A = e^x\) and \(B = \text{logit}(y) e^x\).

background <- function(params,t){
        A = exp(params[[1]])
        B = stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
        return(A + B*sin((2*pi*t)/365.25))
}

background_integral <- function(params,x){
        A = exp(params[[1]])
        B = stats::plogis(params[[2]]) * A
        return((A*x)-B*cos((2*pi*x)/365.25))
}

These functions are then passed to the function fit_hawkes_cbf() alongside the observed times (times) and a list of starting values for both \(\mu(t)\) and the self-exciting components via the argument background_parameters and parameters respectively.

sv = list(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5)
background_sv = list(1,1)
fit <- fit_hawkes_cbf(times = times, parameters = sv,
background = background, background_integral = background_integral, background_parameters = background_sv)

The estimated values of the the transformed \(A\) and \(B\) parameters are returned via fit$background_parameters, the code below transforms them back to the original scale.

title: 3  Marked Hawkes
text:
3.1 A simulated example
The conditional intensity function for the marked Hawkes model implemented in stelfi is given by
\[\lambda(t; m(t)) = \mu + \alpha \Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t}m(\tau_i)\text{exp}(-\beta * (t-\tau_i)) \] where \(\mu\) is the background rate of the process and \(m(t)\) is the temporal mark. The only difference to Equation 2.1 is now that each event has an associated mark \(m(\tau_i)\) that scales the jump sizes (\(\alpha\)) of the self-exciting component of \(\lambda(.)\).
Below data are simulated using the emhawkes package (Lee 2023) where the marks (a vector that scale the jump sizes, starting at 0) are integer values \(\in [1,4]\) for \(t > 0\) and \(0\) for \(t = 0\) (see Section 3.2 for how to simulate using stelfi). The parameter values of the conditional intensity are \(\mu = 1.3\), \(\alpha = 0.4\), and \(\beta = 1.5\). The jump sizes for the possible mark values are shown below.

3.3 The negative log-likelihood
Below the negative log-likelihood of a univariate marked Hawkes process used by stelfi is written using R/RTMB (Kristensen 2024) syntax. The function below returns the negative log-likelihood of a univariate marked Hawkes process, RTMB is used to automatically calculate the gradient and then the function is minimised via nlminb(). See here for and overview of RTMB. This section is for demonstration only, feel free to modify the function as desired. Note that this can be used to fit an unmarked model by setting the vector of marks to be \(\boldsymbol{1}\).

library(RTMB)
univariate_marked_hawkes <- function(params){
    getAll(data, params)
    mu <- exp(log_mu)
    beta <- exp(log_beta)
    alpha <- exp(logit_abratio) / (1 + exp(logit_abratio)) * (beta/mean(marks))
    n <- length(times)
    last <- times[n]
    nll <- 0
    A <- advector(numeric(n)) 
    for(i in 2:n){
        A[i] <- sum(exp(-beta * (times[i] - times[i - 1])) * (marks[i - 1] + A[i - 1]))
    }
    term_3vec <- log(mu + alpha * A)
    nll <- (mu * last) + ((alpha/beta) * (sum(marks) - marks[n] - A[n])) - sum(term_3vec)
    ADREPORT(mu)
    ADREPORT(alpha)
    ADREPORT(beta)
    return(nll)
}

data <- list(times = res$arrival, marks = res$mark)
params <- list(log_mu = log(1.3), logit_abratio = 0.6, log_beta = log(1.5))
obj <- MakeADFun(univariate_marked_hawkes, params, silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
summary(sdreport(obj), "report")

title: 4  Multivariate Hawkes
text:
4.1 A simulated example
A multivariate Hawkes process allows for between- and within-stream self-excitement. In stelfi the conditional intensity for the \(j^{th}\) (\(j = 1, ..., N\)) stream is given by
\[\lambda(t)^{j*} = \mu_j + \Sigma_{k = 1}^N\Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t} \alpha_{jk} e^{(-\beta_j * (t-\tau_i))},\] where \(j, k  \in (1, ..., N)\). Here, \(\alpha_{jk}\) is the excitement caused by the \(k^{th}\) stream on the \(j^{th}\). Therefore, \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) is an \(N \times N\) matrix where the diagonals represent the within-stream excitement and the off-diagonals represent the excitement between streams.
Plotted below are the conditional intensities (\(\lambda_{.}(t), t \in [0,T]\)) of a bivariate Hawkes process with \(\mu = (0.5, 0.9)\), \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) = \(\begin{bmatrix}0.2&0.1 \\0.6&0.5 \\\end{bmatrix}\), and \(\beta = (0.7, 0.9)\). Observed events (n = 33) are shown by the vertical dashes along the x-axis. The intensity of any stream increases immediately after any event occurs (i.e., irrespective of stream) and decays exponentially over time if no event is observed for some period. Typically, herem a jump in intensity due to the occurence of an event in the same stream is called self-excitation (diagonal elements of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\)) and a jump in intensity due to the occurence of an event in a different stream is called cross-excitation (off-diagonal elements of \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\)).
Simulating data from the hawkes package Zaatour (2014) with \(\mu = (0.5, 0.9)\), \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) = \(\begin{bmatrix}0.2&0.1 \\0.6&0.5 \\\end{bmatrix}\), and \(\beta = (0.7, 0.9)\) over the time period \(t\in [0,50)\).
mu <- c(0.5, 0.9)
alpha <- matrix(c(0.2, 0.1 ,0.6, 0.5), byrow = TRUE, nrow = 2)
beta <- c(0.7, 0.9)
set.seed(1)
sim <- hawkes::simulateHawkes(mu, alpha, beta, 500)
To fit the model in stelfi the fit_mhawkes() function is used with the arguments times (a numeric vector of event times), stream (a character vector specifying the stream ID of each observation in times), and a lit of starting value for the parameters (parameters).

data <- data[order(data$times),]
## list of starting values

fit <- stelfi::fit_mhawkes(times = data$times, stream = data$stream, parameters = sv)

title: 5  Spatial log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
5.1 Delauney triangluations when fitting LGCP models
A log-Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP) is a doubly stochastic spatial point process. In the simplest case, the intensity of the point process over space is given by \[\Lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s) + \epsilon)\] where \(\beta_0\) is a constant, known as the intercept, \(G(s)\) is a Gaussian Markov Random Field (GMRF) and \(\epsilon\) an error term.
Plotted below is a realisation of a LGCP within a disc shaped region overlain on the latent GMRF.
Following the Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE) approach proposed by Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011) a Matérn covariance function is assumed for \(G(s)\):
\[C(r; \sigma, \kappa) = \frac{\sigma^2}{2^{\nu-1} \Gamma(\nu)} (\kappa \:r)^\nu K_\nu(\kappa \: r)\]
where \(\kappa\) is a scaling parameter and \(\sigma^2\) is the marginal variance (\(\nu\) is typically fixed, see Lindgren, Rue, and Lindström (2011)). Rather than the scaling parameter, a range parameter \(r=\frac{\sqrt{8}}{\kappa}\) is typically interpreted (corresponding to correlations near 0.1 at the distance \(r\)). The standard deviation is given as \(\sigma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\kappa^2\tau^2}}\). In the figure above \(\beta = 3\), \(\text{log}(\tau) = 1.6\), and \(\text{log}(\kappa) = 1.95\).
The SPDE approach represents the continuous Gaussian field \(G(s)\) by a GMRF defined on the nodes of a Delauney triangulation (a mesh) of the study region. The field is then interpolated linearly between nodes, so the mesh controls both how finely the field can vary in space and how much computation is needed. In stelfi (and inlabru) the mesh is built using the fmesher package, the key arguments of fmesher::fm_mesh_2d() are:
There is a trade-off. A mesh that is too coarse cannot capture the spatial variation in the field (and, in particular, variation at a scale smaller than the triangles is lost), while a mesh that is too fine is slow and memory-hungry, and can lead to an unstable fit when there is little information in the data about fine-scale structure. A common rule of thumb is that max.edge should be smaller than (roughly a fifth of) the spatial range of the field. In practice it is good to check that your inference is not sensitive to the mesh, this is demonstrated in Section 5.5.5.
Note that the mesh is a model for the latent field only, the events themselves are always at their observed locations and the region over which the intensity is integrated is given by the sf argument of fit_lgcp().

title: 5  Spatial log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
loc or loc.domain: locations (usually the observed events) that the mesh is built around, so there are mesh nodes close to the data.
boundary: (optional) a polygon the mesh should be constrained to, for example the study region.
max.edge: the largest allowed triangle edge length. A vector of length two, c(inner, outer), gives a finer mesh inside the domain and a coarser mesh in an outer extension.
cutoff: the minimum allowed distance between any two nodes. Points closer together than this are merged to a single node, which avoids lots of tiny triangles where events are clustered.

title: 5  Spatial log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
5.3 The negative log-likelihood
Below the negative log-likelihood of a simple (spatial) LGCP is written using R/RTMB (Kristensen 2024) syntax, in the same way as for the marked Hawkes process (see Section 3.3). RTMB is used to automatically calculate the gradient, the GMRF is treated as a random effect and integrated out using the Laplace approximation, and the function is then minimised via nlminb(). This section is for demonstration only, feel free to modify the function as desired. The sasquatch data and mesh from the applied example above are used so that the result can be compared directly with fit_lgcp().
Given the events \(s_1, ..., s_n\) in a domain \(D\), the log-likelihood of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\lambda(s)=\text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s))\) is \[\log L = \sum_{j=1}^n \log \lambda(s_j) - \int_D \lambda(s)\,ds.\] The field is represented on the mesh as \(G(s) = \sum_i \psi_i(s) x_i\), where \(\psi_i\) are the piecewise linear basis functions and \(\boldsymbol{x} \sim \text{N}(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{Q}^{-1})\). For the SPDE with \(\nu = 1\) the precision matrix is \[\boldsymbol{Q} = \tau^2(\kappa^4 \boldsymbol{C} + 2\kappa^2 \boldsymbol{G} + \boldsymbol{G}\boldsymbol{C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{G}),\] where \(\boldsymbol{C}\) and \(\boldsymbol{G}\) are the (lumped) mass and stiffness matrices of the mesh. To evaluate the likelihood two ingredients are needed:

a sparse “projection” matrix \(\boldsymbol{A}\) that maps the values at the mesh nodes to any set of locations, i.e., \(G(s_j) = (\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x})_j\) (using fm_basis()), and
a set of integration points with weights (using fm_int()) so that the integral over the domain is approximated by a weighted sum \(\int_D \lambda(s)ds \approx \sum_k w_k \lambda(u_k)\). The weights sum to the area of \(D\), so the integral only covers the domain and not the outer extension of the mesh.


library(RTMB)
## the domain as a single polygon with no CRS (to match the mesh)
us_dom <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_union(sf::st_set_crs(sf::st_geometry(us), NA)))
## SPDE matrices (Matern, nu = 1) on the mesh
fem <- fmesher::fm_fem(smesh, order = 2)
as_T <- function(M) as(as(M, "generalMatrix"), "TsparseMatrix")
## integration points and weights over the domain
ips <- fmesher::fm_int(smesh, samplers = us_dom)
ip_xy <- sf::st_coordinates(ips)[, 1:2]
## data for the template
data <- list(M0 = as_T(fem$c0), M1 = as_T(fem$g1), M2 = as_T(fem$g2),
             A_pts = fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = as.matrix(locs[, 1:2])),
             A_ips = fmesher::fm_basis(smesh, loc = ip_xy),
             w = ips$weight)


lgcp_nll <- function(params){
    getAll(data, params)
    tau <- exp(log_tau)
    kappa <- exp(log_kappa)
    ## SPDE precision matrix of the field at the mesh nodes
    Q <- tau^2 * (kappa^4 * M0 + 2 * kappa^2 * M1 + M2)
    ## prior for the random field
    nll <- -dgmrf(x, 0, Q, log = TRUE)
    ## log-intensity at the events and at the integration points
    eta_pts <- beta + A_pts %*% x
    eta_ips <- beta + A_ips %*% x
    ## point process log-likelihood: sum of log-intensity at events minus the integral
    nll <- nll - sum(eta_pts) + sum(w * exp(eta_ips))
    ## range and marginal standard deviation of the field
    spatial_range <- sqrt(8) / kappa
    sd_field <- 1 / sqrt(4 * pi * kappa^2 * tau^2)
    ADREPORT(beta)
    ADREPORT(spatial_range)
    ADREPORT(sd_field)
    return(nll)
}

The random field x (one value per mesh node) is declared as a random effect through random = "x". The starting value for \(\beta_0\) is the log of the average number of events per unit area.

params <- list(beta = log(nrow(locs) / sum(data$w)), log_tau = log(1),
               log_kappa = log(1), x = rep(0, smesh$n))
obj <- MakeADFun(lgcp_nll, params, random = "x", silent = TRUE)
opt <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr)
sdr <- sdreport(obj)
summary(sdr, "report")

                Estimate Std. Error
beta          -0.6251042  0.4542078
spatial_range 10.4616015  1.8515722
sd_field       1.2656670  0.1764758


Compared to the estimates from stelfi (rows 1, 4 and 5 are \(\beta_0\), \(r\), and \(\sigma\)) the numbers should be close, but not identical, since the two implementations discretise the events and the integral in slightly different ways.

get_coefs(fit)[c(1, 4, 5), ]

        Estimate Std. Error
beta  -0.7659374  0.3558810
range  7.3430022  1.1089110
stdev  1.3491824  0.1480772


The estimated field (the posterior mode of the random effects) can be extracted and plotted as before.

x_hat <- as.list(sdr, "Estimate")$x
show_field(x_hat, smesh = smesh, sf = us, clip = TRUE) + ggplot2::theme_classic()








To include covariates replace beta with a vector of coefficients and the intercept in both eta_pts and eta_ips with a design matrix times that vector, e.g., X_pts %*% beta and X_ips %*% beta, where the covariates are evaluated at the events and at the integration points (or, as in fit_lgcp(), at the mesh nodes and then projected using A_pts and A_ips).

title: 5  Spatial log-Gaussian Cox process
text:
5.4 Assessing model fit
Having fitted a LGCP it is sensible to ask whether data simulated from the fitted model look like the data we observed. One way to do this is to compare summary functions of the observed point pattern to those of patterns simulated from the fitted model, using the spatstat package. Here this is done for the sasquatch model above using two nearest-neighbour type summaries:

the \(G\) function, the distribution function of the distance from a typical event to its nearest other event. For a clustered pattern \(G(r)\) rises faster than that of a completely spatially random (Poisson) pattern since events tend to have a close neighbour.
the \(F\) function (the empty space function), the distribution function of the distance from a fixed arbitrary location to the nearest event. For a clustered pattern \(F(r)\) rises more slowly than that of a Poisson pattern since there are large empty gaps between clusters.

If the fitted LGCP is adequate, the observed curves should lie within the envelope formed by the curves of the simulated patterns.

5.4.1 Preparing the data
Distances need to be measured in a planar (projected) coordinate system rather than in degrees of latitude and longitude. The US boundary and the sightings are projected (here to the Conus Albers projection, EPSG:5070) and converted from metres to kilometres. The model is then refitted on this scale, so the range \(r\) of the field is on the kilometre scale too.

library(spatstat.geom)
library(spatstat.explore)
## project the US boundary and convert from metres to km
us_km <- sf::st_transform(us, crs = 5070)
sf::st_geometry(us_km) <- sf::st_geometry(us_km) / 1000
us_window <- as.owin(sf::st_union(us_km))
## project the sightings and convert from metres to km
locs_km <- sf::st_transform(sasquatch, crs = 5070) |>
    sf::st_coordinates() |>
    as.data.frame()
names(locs_km) <- c("x", "y")
locs_km <- locs_km / 1000
## mesh (in km) and model fit
smesh_km <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs_km[, 1:2], max.edge = 200, cutoff = 100)
fit_km <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = us_km, smesh = smesh_km,
                   parameters = c(beta = 0, log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)))
coefs <- get_coefs(fit_km)
coefs

            Estimate  Std. Error
beta       -9.882848   0.3692612
log_tau     4.036590   0.1061427
log_kappa  -5.584941   0.1597940
range     753.449133 120.3966852
stdev       1.326891   0.1533704


The observed events are converted to a spatstat point pattern (ppp). Some sightings share exactly the same location, which would give nearest-neighbour distances of exactly zero, so the pattern is jittered slightly using rjitter().

set.seed(1)
obs_ppp <- ppp(x = locs_km$x, y = locs_km$y, window = us_window)
obs_ppp_clean <- rjitter(obs_ppp, retry = TRUE)



5.4.2 Simulating from the fitted model
The function below simulates one point pattern from the fitted LGCP using sim_lgcp() and the estimated parameters. The simulated counts are per mesh node, so each node is repeated as many times as it has simulated events (rep()) and the resulting pattern is jittered so that events are spread around the node rather than stacked on top of it. The jitter radius here is half the mesh cutoff (the minimum distance between nodes) so that events stay close to the node they were simulated at.

generate_simulated_ppp <- function() {
    sim <- sim_lgcp(sf = us_km, smesh = smesh_km,
                    parameters = c(beta = coefs[1, 1],
                                   log_tau = coefs[2, 1],
                                   log_kappa = coefs[3, 1]))
    ## need at least two events to measure a nearest-neighbour distance
    if(sum(sim$y) < 2) return(NULL)
    idx <- rep(1:nrow(smesh_km$loc), times = sim$y)
    sim_coords <- smesh_km$loc[idx, 1:2]
    sim_ppp <- ppp(x = sim_coords[, 1], y = sim_coords[, 2],
                   window = us_window, check = FALSE)
    rjitter(sim_ppp, radius = 50, retry = TRUE)
}

A first look is to compare the observed \(G\) function to that of a couple of simulated patterns (in grey).

set.seed(2)
sim_list <- lapply(1:2, function(i) generate_simulated_ppp())
g_obs <- Gest(obs_ppp_clean)
plot(g_obs$r, g_obs$km, type = "l", xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "G(r)")
for(s in sim_list) {
    g_sim <- Gest(s)
    lines(g_sim$r, g_sim$km, col = "grey")
}










5.4.3 Simulation envelopes
Two simulations are not enough to say anything formal. A simulation envelope uses many simulated patterns, and for each distance \(r\) gives the range of the simulated summary function (here the pointwise minimum and maximum). With \(n_{sim} = 39\) simulations a pointwise envelope based on the min and max corresponds to a two-sided test with significance level \(2 / (n_{sim} + 1) = 0.05\) at each \(r\) (more simulations are preferable, e.g., 99, but take longer). Passing the list of LGCP simulations to the simulate argument of envelope() is important, otherwise the envelope is formed from completely spatially random patterns and instead tests the null of no spatial structure at all.

set.seed(3)
n_simulations <- 39
sim_list <- lapply(1:n_simulations, function(i) generate_simulated_ppp())
sim_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), sim_list)

g_envelope <- envelope(Y = obs_ppp_clean, fun = Gest,
                       simulate = sim_list, nsim = length(sim_list),
                       savefuns = TRUE)

Extracting 39 point patterns from list  ...

plot(g_envelope, . ~ r, main = "Sasquatch LGCP G-function envelope",
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "G(r)", legend = TRUE)








In the plot the solid black line is the observed \(G(r)\), the dashed line is the mean of the simulated patterns, and the grey band is the envelope. Where the observed curve leaves the band the fitted model is not reproducing the nearest-neighbour structure of the data. The same can be done for the empty space function.

section: 5.5 An applied example: terrorism events in Iraq
text:
5.5 An applied example: terrorism events in Iraq
The iraq_terrorism data (see ?iraq_terrorism) are the locations and years of terrorism events in Iraq (with the population density at each event location). This example is used to (1) show the full stelfi workflow for a region with an awkward boundary, (2) compare stelfi with inlabru (Bachl et al. (2019)) on the same data and the same mesh, (3) explore how sensitive inference is to the mesh, and (4) include covariates in the intensity. For the spatiotemporal version of this analysis see Section 7.1.

5.5.1 Preparing the data
The event locations are given as longitude/latitude. As in the sasquatch example above, the data are projected to a planar coordinate system, here UTM zone 38N (EPSG:32638), which covers most of Iraq, and converted to kilometres. Working in kilometres rather than metres keeps the numbers in the optimisation well-scaled and gives parameters that are easy to interpret (the intensity is the expected number of events per km\(^2\) and the range is in km). The boundary of Iraq is obtained from the rnaturalearth package (which also requires rnaturalearthdata) and transformed in exactly the same way.

require(sf)
data("iraq_terrorism", package = "stelfi")
## event locations (lon/lat) -> UTM zone 38N -> km
iraq_coordinates <- sf::st_coordinates(iraq_terrorism) |> as.data.frame()
names(iraq_coordinates) <- c("Longitude", "Latitude")
points_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(iraq_coordinates, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)
points_utm <- sf::st_transform(points_sf, crs = 32638)
locs_km <- as.data.frame(sf::st_coordinates(points_utm) / 1000)
names(locs_km) <- c("x", "y")
## sf version of the events (used by inlabru later)
points_km <- sf::st_as_sf(locs_km, coords = c("x", "y"))
## observation window: the boundary of Iraq in the same coordinates
iraq_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(country = "Iraq", scale = "medium",
                                       returnclass = "sf") |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638) |>
    sf::st_union()                     ## collapse to a single polygon
iraq_sf_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(iraq_sf) / 1000)
## once in km the coordinates are just planar numbers, so drop the CRS everywhere
## so that the events, the boundary and the mesh are all treated consistently
sf::st_crs(iraq_sf_km) <- NA



5.5.2 Building the meshes
Three triangulations are built, constrained to the boundary of Iraq (boundary = fm_as_segm(...)) and around the observed events. Each has a finer inner and coarser outer part (max.edge = c(inner, outer)). The same three meshes are used for both stelfi and inlabru so that any difference in the results is not due to the mesh.

mesh_args <- list(coarse = list(max.edge = c(60, 200), cutoff = 15),
                  medium = list(max.edge = c(40, 200), cutoff = 5),
                  fine   = list(max.edge = c(10, 100), cutoff = 2))
meshes <- lapply(mesh_args, function(a) {
    fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs_km[, 1:2],
                        boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(iraq_sf_km),
                        max.edge = a$max.edge, cutoff = a$cutoff)
})
## number of nodes in each mesh
sapply(meshes, function(m) m$n)

coarse medium   fine 
   598   1568  11940 


The medium mesh, the events (points), and the boundary of Iraq (blue) are shown below.

ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = mesh_2_sf(meshes$medium), fill = NA) +
    geom_sf(data = iraq_sf_km, fill = NA, col = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_sf(data = points_km, size = 0.5) +
    theme_void()










5.5.3 Fitting with stelfi
A sensible starting value for the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the log of the average number of events per unit area (the log intensity of a flat surface). The starting values for \(\log(\tau)\) and \(\log(\kappa)\) are left at 0 (as before).

area_km2 <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(iraq_sf_km))
beta_start <- log(nrow(locs_km) / area_km2)
start <- c(beta = beta_start, log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1))
## fit the model for each of the three meshes
fits_stelfi <- lapply(meshes, function(m) {
    fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = m, parameters = start)
})
get_coefs(fits_stelfi$medium)

beta      -10.4615767 0.39736153
log_tau     0.1693602 0.06063699
log_kappa  -2.6639452 0.07788022
range      40.5958551 3.16161410
stdev       3.4180592 0.18938261


The estimated GMRF and the intensity surface (events per km\(^2\)) are plotted using show_field() (after get_fields()) and show_lambda() as before.

get_fields(fits_stelfi$medium, meshes$medium) |>
    show_field(smesh = meshes$medium, sf = iraq_sf_km, clip = TRUE) + theme_classic()









show_lambda(fits_stelfi$medium, smesh = meshes$medium, sf = iraq_sf_km, clip = TRUE) +
    theme_classic()










5.5.4 Comparing with inlabru
inlabru fits the same model, but there are some important differences to bear in mind when comparing the results:

stelfi is a maximum likelihood approach (the field is integrated out using the Laplace approximation via TMB) so there are no priors and estimates are accompanied by standard errors. inlabru is Bayesian (using INLA), so priors are required for the field and the reported values are posterior means and standard deviations. Here penalised complexity priors are used via inla.spde2.pcmatern(), prior.range = c(5, 0.01) meaning \(P(r < 5\text{ km}) = 0.01\) and prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01) meaning \(P(\sigma > 10) = 0.01\). These are deliberately weak.
To make inlabru as close as possible to a maximum likelihood fit, the hyperparameters are not integrated over (int.strategy = "eb", empirical Bayes) and a Gaussian approximation is used (strategy = "gaussian"). The remaining options (diagonal, control.vb) are numerical settings.
The parameterisation of the Matérn field differs, but the quantities that can be compared directly are the intercept \(\beta_0\), the range \(r\), and the marginal standard deviation \(\sigma\). These correspond to rows 1, 4, and 5 of get_coefs() from stelfi and to Intercept, Range for mySmooth and Stdev for mySmooth from inlabru. Because the coordinates are in km in both, \(\beta_0\) is the log intensity per km\(^2\) in both and \(r\) is in km.


require(inlabru)
require(INLA)

fit_bru <- function(mesh) {
    matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                                        prior.sigma = c(10, 0.01),
                                        prior.range = c(5, 0.01))
    ## latent field + intercept
    cmp <- geometry ~ mySmooth(geometry, model = matern) + Intercept(1)
    ## fit the LGCP, integrating the intensity over the boundary of Iraq (samplers)
    inlabru::lgcp(cmp, data = points_km, samplers = iraq_sf_km,
                  domain = list(geometry = mesh),
                  options = inlabru::bru_options(
                      control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb",
                                          strategy = "gaussian",
                                          diagonal = 1e-4,
                                          control.vb = list(enable = FALSE))))
}
fits_inlabru <- lapply(meshes, fit_bru)
fits_inlabru$medium$summary.fixed
fits_inlabru$medium$summary.hyperpar

The table below gives the estimates (standard error for stelfi, posterior standard deviation for inlabru in brackets) for each mesh.

fmt <- function(x) {
    x <- as.numeric(x)
    paste0(round(x[1], 3), " (", round(x[2], 3), ")")
}
rows <- lapply(names(meshes), function(m) {
    s <- get_coefs(fits_stelfi[[m]])[c(1, 4, 5), 1:2]
    b <- rbind(fits_inlabru[[m]]$summary.fixed[, 1:2],
               fits_inlabru[[m]]$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2])
    data.frame(mesh = m, package = c("stelfi", "inlabru"),
               beta0 = c(fmt(s[1, ]), fmt(b[1, ])),
               range = c(fmt(s[2, ]), fmt(b[2, ])),
               sigma = c(fmt(s[3, ]), fmt(b[3, ])))
})
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, rows),
             col.names = c("Mesh", "Package", "$\\beta_0$", "$r$", "$\\sigma$"),
             escape = FALSE)

When reading the table look for: (1) agreement between packages for a given mesh, the estimates will not be identical (the methods and the parameterisation differ, and inlabru uses priors) but they should tell the same story about the baseline intensity, the scale of spatial dependence, and the amount of spatial variation; and (2) agreement across meshes for a given package, discussed next.


5.5.5 Sensitivity to the mesh
The estimates for the three meshes are compared using the output from stelfi (the same can be done using the inlabru fits above). The number of nodes, and so the computational cost, increases a lot from the coarse to fine mesh.

coefs_by_mesh <- lapply(fits_stelfi, function(f) get_coefs(f)[c(1, 4, 5), 1:2])
do.call(cbind, lapply(names(coefs_by_mesh), function(m) {
    x <- round(coefs_by_mesh[[m]], 3)
    colnames(x) <- paste(m, colnames(x))
    x
}))

range          87.421            10.276          40.596             3.162
stdev           2.960             0.239           3.418             0.189

The fitted intensity surfaces can also be compared side by side. If the mesh is adequate the large scale pattern of the intensity (hot spots) should be similar for all three, the finer mesh will mainly add local detail.

lambdas <- lapply(names(meshes), function(m) {
    show_lambda(fits_stelfi[[m]], smesh = meshes[[m]], sf = iraq_sf_km, clip = TRUE) +
        ggplot2::theme_void() + ggplot2::ggtitle(m)
})
patchwork::wrap_plots(lambdas, nrow = 1)








If the range and standard deviation change noticeably between meshes then the coarse mesh is too coarse to represent the field (the estimated range will tend to be larger as small scale variation cannot be captured). A fine mesh near to or finer than the true range of the field should give estimates that are stable, if the estimates are still changing from the medium to the fine mesh then try an even finer mesh. The additional computational cost of a fine mesh is usually not worth it once the estimates have stabilised.


5.5.6 Including covariates
Covariates can be included in the log-intensity, \(\Lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1(s) + ... + G(s))\), using the covariates argument of fit_lgcp(). The covariates must be supplied as a matrix with one column per covariate and one row per node of the mesh (i.e., the value of the covariate at each of the smesh$n nodes), and the starting value beta becomes a vector of length one (the intercept) plus the number of covariates. Below the medium mesh is used.

smesh <- meshes$medium


5.5.6.1 Distance to Baghdad
Here the covariate is the Euclidean distance (in km) from each mesh node to Baghdad (33°18′N, 44°24′E, or 33.30, 44.40 in decimal degrees). The covariate is standardised (scale()) so the coefficient is the change in log-intensity per standard deviation increase in distance, and so the optimiser works with parameters on a similar scale.

baghdad <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(Longitude = 44.40, Latitude = 33.30),
                        coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638)
baghdad_km <- sf::st_coordinates(baghdad) / 1000
## distance (km) from every mesh node to Baghdad
mesh_coords <- smesh$loc[, 1:2]
baghdad_dist <- sqrt((mesh_coords[, 1] - baghdad_km[1])^2 +
                     (mesh_coords[, 2] - baghdad_km[2])^2)
baghdad_scaled <- as.matrix(scale(baghdad_dist))
sd(baghdad_dist) ## km per unit of the scaled covariate

[1] 142.8089



fit_baghdad <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = smesh,
                        parameters = list(beta = c(beta_start, 0),
                                          log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)),
                        covariates = baghdad_scaled)
get_coefs(fit_baghdad)

             Estimate Std. Error
beta      -10.1442624 0.34778483
beta       -1.3433509 0.28134940
log_tau     0.1179046 0.06460445
log_kappa  -2.5396546 0.07987871
range      35.8511413 2.86374286
stdev       3.1779551 0.16668768


The coefficient beta (second element) is the change in the log-intensity of events per standard deviation (see above, in km) increase in distance from Baghdad, so \(\text{exp}(\beta_1)\) is the multiplicative change in the intensity. A negative coefficient means events are more intense closer to Baghdad. Note that the mesh extends beyond the boundary of Iraq, so the standardisation uses nodes that are outside the country too.


5.5.6.2 Population density
Population density is only observed at the event locations in these data, not at the mesh nodes, so it has to be interpolated to the mesh nodes. Here inverse distance weighting (gstat::idw()) is used to predict the population density at each node from the values at the events (any reasonable interpolation, such as kernel smoothing or using the value from the nearest event, would do, it does not need to be perfect).

require(gstat)
## events with their population density (km coordinates, no CRS)
points_pop <- points_km
points_pop$popdensity <- iraq_terrorism$popdensity
## mesh nodes as an sf object
mesh_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(as.data.frame(smesh$loc[, 1:2]) |> setNames(c("x", "y")),
                        coords = c("x", "y"))
## interpolate (inverse distance weighted) onto the mesh nodes
idw_fit <- gstat::idw(formula = popdensity ~ 1, locations = points_pop,
                      newdata = mesh_sf, debug.level = 0)
scaled_popdensity <- as.matrix(scale(idw_fit$var1.pred))


fit_pop <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = smesh,
                    parameters = list(beta = c(beta_start, 0),
                                      log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1)),
                    covariates = scaled_popdensity)
get_coefs(fit_pop)

             Estimate Std. Error
beta      -9.36865654 0.27424276
beta      -1.58631396 0.14909077
log_tau    0.05934407 0.07069666
log_kappa -2.36289605 0.08056003
range     30.04261333 2.42023386
stdev      2.82367676 0.13280817








Note



Care is needed when interpreting this coefficient. Because the population density is only known at the events the interpolated covariate surface is informed only by where events happened, not by where people live in general. It is therefore not an independent description of the population, and a negative (or otherwise surprising) coefficient does not necessarily mean that fewer events occur in more densely populated places. A gridded population density raster that is available over the whole of Iraq would be preferable if available. It is also worth remembering that the GMRF can absorb spatial structure shared with the covariate (spatial confounding), so check the standard error of the coefficient, and compare the model with and without the covariate (e.g., using AIC() on the fitted objects or looking at how much the field changes).

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.1 Set up
A good way to compare two methods for fitting the same model is to simulate data where the true parameter values are known, fit the model with both methods, and see how well each recovers the truth. Repeating this many times shows how the estimators behave on average, rather than for a single dataset. In this chapter many spatial log-Gaussian Cox processes (see Chapter 5) are simulated and fitted using stelfi and inlabru (Bachl et al. (2019)), and the following are compared:
The parameters of interest are the intercept \(\beta_0\), the range \(r = \sqrt{8}/\kappa\) and the marginal standard deviation \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{4\pi\kappa^2\tau^2}\) of the field (see Chapter 5).

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.1.1 The domain and the true parameter values
As in Chapter 5 the domain is a disc (of radius 1). The true values are chosen so that there is a clear spatial signal to recover: a range of 0.5 (a quarter of the width of the domain) and a marginal standard deviation of 1 for the field. The intercept is 4 so that, on average, a few hundred events are observed in each simulated dataset. The values of \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\) that stelfi works with follow by rearranging the formulas for \(r\) and \(\sigma\).

require(stelfi)
require(ggplot2)
## domain
disc_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(spatstat.geom::disc())
bb <- sf::st_bbox(disc_sf)
area <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(disc_sf))
## true values of the parameters of interest
true_beta <- 4; true_range <- 0.5; true_sigma <- 1
## the corresponding values of kappa and tau
true_kappa <- sqrt(8) / true_range
true_tau <- 1 / (true_sigma * sqrt(4 * pi) * true_kappa)
true_par <- c(beta = true_beta, log_tau = log(true_tau), log_kappa = log(true_kappa))
round(true_par, 3)

     beta   log_tau log_kappa 
    4.000    -2.998     1.733 




6.1.2 Two meshes
Two triangulations of the domain are used (see Section 5.1). A fine mesh is used to simulate the data and a coarser mesh to fit the models. Simulating and fitting on the same mesh would be a little too kind to the methods (the simulated field would be exactly representable by the model), whereas in practice the true field is never exactly the piecewise linear field on the mesh you choose. The fitting mesh has a max.edge of 0.1, which is a fifth of the true range of 0.5 (the rule of thumb from Section 5.1), and is the same for every replicate and for both packages.

loc_domain <- sf::st_coordinates(disc_sf)[, 1:2]
mesh_sim <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc.domain = loc_domain, max.edge = c(0.05, 0.3),
                                offset = c(0.05, 0.4), cutoff = 0.01)
mesh_fit <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc.domain = loc_domain, max.edge = c(0.1, 0.3),
                                offset = c(0.05, 0.4), cutoff = 0.03)
c(simulation = mesh_sim$n, fitting = mesh_fit$n)

simulation    fitting 
      4084       1129

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.2 Simulating the data
A realisation of the Gaussian field on the fine mesh is simulated using sim_lgcp(). Rather than placing events at the mesh nodes, events are then simulated at continuous locations from the intensity \(\lambda(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G(s))\) (the field is interpolated between nodes) by thinning:

simulate a homogeneous Poisson process with rate \(\lambda_{max} = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + \text{max}_i x_i)\), which is at least as large as the intensity everywhere, over the bounding box of the domain,
keep only the points inside the domain, and
keep each remaining point \(s\) with probability \(\lambda(s) / \lambda_{max}\).

The retained points are an exact draw from the LGCP given the field.

sim_events <- function() {
    ## 1. simulate the field (values at the nodes of the fine mesh)
    s <- sim_lgcp(parameters = true_par, sf = disc_sf, smesh = mesh_sim)
    x <- as.vector(s$x)
    ## 2. homogeneous Poisson process with the maximum rate over the bounding box
    lambda_max <- exp(true_beta + max(x))
    area_bb <- (bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"]) * (bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"])
    n0 <- rpois(1, lambda_max * area_bb)
    cand <- data.frame(x = runif(n0, bb["xmin"], bb["xmax"]),
                       y = runif(n0, bb["ymin"], bb["ymax"]))
    ## keep points inside the domain
    inside <- lengths(sf::st_intersects(sf::st_as_sf(cand, coords = c("x", "y")),
                                        disc_sf)) > 0
    cand <- cand[inside, ]
    ## 3. thin: keep with probability lambda(s) / lambda_max
    A <- fmesher::fm_basis(mesh_sim, loc = as.matrix(cand))
    lambda <- exp(true_beta + as.vector(A %*% x))
    cand[runif(nrow(cand)) < lambda / lambda_max, ]
}

One simulated dataset is shown below.

set.seed(1)
locs <- sim_events()
nrow(locs)

[1] 385

ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = disc_sf, fill = NA) +
    geom_point(data = locs, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
    theme_void()














Note



The field is simulated using stelfi’s own parameterisation of the Matérn field. This is the standard SPDE field with a range \(r\) and marginal standard deviation \(\sigma\) related to \(\kappa\) and \(\tau\) as above, which is also what inlabru models via inla.spde2.pcmatern(). Both packages are therefore fitting a model that is correct up to the mesh, but it is worth knowing that the simulator and one of the fitting methods share code.

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.3 Fitting the models

6.3.1 stelfi
The same default-type starting values are used for every dataset (as a user would): \(\log(\tau) = \log(\kappa) = 0\) and the intercept is started at the log of the average number of events per unit area.

start_values <- function(n) {
    c(beta = log(n / area), log_tau = log(1), log_kappa = log(1))
}
fit <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs, sf = disc_sf, smesh = mesh_fit,
                parameters = start_values(nrow(locs)))
get_coefs(fit)

            Estimate Std. Error
beta       4.5320065  0.2072005
log_tau   -2.9106912  0.2271913
log_kappa  1.8970641  0.2477322
range      0.4242878  0.1051098
stdev      0.7773341  0.1088299


Rows 1, 4 and 5 of get_coefs() are \(\beta_0\), \(r\), and \(\sigma\). stelfi gives estimates with standard errors, and a 95% Wald interval is made from these. The range and standard deviation are positive so the interval is calculated on the log scale (the standard error of the log of an estimate is approximately the standard error divided by the estimate, the delta method) and transformed back, this stops intervals going below zero.

tidy_stelfi <- function(fit) {
    cf <- as.matrix(get_coefs(fit)[c(1, 4, 5), 1:2])
    est <- unname(cf[, 1]); se <- unname(cf[, 2])
    z <- 1.96
    data.frame(param = c("beta", "range", "sigma"), est = est,
               lower = c(est[1] - z * se[1], est[2:3] * exp(-z * se[2:3] / est[2:3])),
               upper = c(est[1] + z * se[1], est[2:3] * exp( z * se[2:3] / est[2:3])))
}
tidy_stelfi(fit)

  param       est     lower     upper
1  beta 4.5320065 4.1258934 4.9381195
2 range 0.4242878 0.2610878 0.6895003
3 sigma 0.7773341 0.5907911 1.0227783




6.3.2 inlabru
inlabru is Bayesian so priors are needed for the field. Penalised complexity priors are used (as in Section 5.5) and are set to be weak relative to the domain, prior.range = c(0.05, 0.01) means \(P(r < 0.05) = 0.01\) and prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01) means \(P(\sigma > 5) = 0.01\). Note that the true values (0.5 and 1) are not at the centre of the priors, but neither are they in the tails.
Two configurations of inlabru are compared. The first, "inlabru (eb)", is the one used in Section 5.5: the hyperparameters are not integrated over (empirical Bayes) and a Gaussian approximation is used, which is the closest to maximum likelihood. The second, "inlabru (default)", uses the default settings, which integrate over the uncertainty in the hyperparameters (the range and standard deviation) and so is the “full” Bayesian answer. For inlabru the estimate is the posterior mean and the interval is the 95% credible interval. This is not the same thing as a confidence interval, but if the priors are weak the two should be similar and coverage is still an informative thing to check.

require(inlabru)
require(INLA)

matern <- INLA::inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh_fit,
                                    prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01),
                                    prior.range = c(0.05, 0.01))
cmp <- geometry ~ mySmooth(geometry, model = matern) + Intercept(1)

fit_inlabru <- function(locs, config = c("eb", "default")) {
    config <- match.arg(config)
    opts <- if (config == "eb") {
        inlabru::bru_options(control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb",
                                                 strategy = "gaussian",
                                                 diagonal = 1e-4,
                                                 control.vb = list(enable = FALSE)))
    } else {
        inlabru::bru_options()
    }
    pts <- sf::st_as_sf(locs, coords = c("x", "y"))
    inlabru::lgcp(cmp, data = pts, samplers = disc_sf,
                  domain = list(geometry = mesh_fit), options = opts)
}

tidy_inlabru <- function(fit) {
    cols <- c("mean", "0.025quant", "0.975quant")
    tab <- rbind(fit$summary.fixed["Intercept", cols],
                 fit$summary.hyperpar["Range for mySmooth", cols],
                 fit$summary.hyperpar["Stdev for mySmooth", cols])
    data.frame(param = c("beta", "range", "sigma"), est = tab[, 1],
               lower = tab[, 2], upper = tab[, 3])
}

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.4 Running the study
For each replicate a dataset is simulated and then fitted by the three methods. Each fit is wrapped so that if it fails (an error, or non-finite estimates or intervals, such as a standard error that cannot be calculated) the replicate is recorded as a failure instead of stopping the whole study, since the failure rate is itself part of the comparison. The time taken for each fit is recorded too (so this is the time for the fit alone, not for simulation). The seed is set to the replicate number, so any single replicate can be reproduced.

attempt <- function(method, fit_fun, tidy_fun) {
    time <- system.time(fit <- try(suppressMessages(fit_fun()), silent = TRUE))[["elapsed"]]
    res <- if (inherits(fit, "try-error")) NULL else try(tidy_fun(fit), silent = TRUE)
    ok <- !is.null(res) && !inherits(res, "try-error") &&
        all(is.finite(unlist(res[, c("est", "lower", "upper")])))
    if (is.null(res) || inherits(res, "try-error")) {
        res <- data.frame(param = c("beta", "range", "sigma"),
                          est = NA_real_, lower = NA_real_, upper = NA_real_)
    }
    data.frame(method = method, res, time = time, ok = ok)
}

run_one <- function(r) {
    set.seed(r)
    locs <- sim_events()
    out <- rbind(
        attempt("stelfi",
                function() fit_lgcp(locs = locs, sf = disc_sf, smesh = mesh_fit,
                                    parameters = start_values(nrow(locs))),
                tidy_stelfi),
        attempt("inlabru (eb)", function() fit_inlabru(locs, "eb"), tidy_inlabru),
        attempt("inlabru (default)", function() fit_inlabru(locs, "default"), tidy_inlabru))
    data.frame(rep = r, n_events = nrow(locs), out)
}

n_rep <- 100
results <- do.call(rbind, pbapply::pblapply(1:n_rep, run_one))
saveRDS(results, "recovery-results.rds")

Increasing n_rep reduces the Monte Carlo error of the summaries, with 100 replicates the Monte Carlo standard error of an estimated coverage of 95% is about 2 percentage points (\(\sqrt{0.95 \times 0.05 / 100}\)), so coverages between roughly 91% and 99% cannot be distinguished from 95%. For a final version of the chapter 500 or more replicates are better. The replicates are independent so can be run in parallel (e.g., using parallel::mclapply() on Linux/macOS).

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.5 Results

6.5.1 Failures and run time
The failure rate is the proportion of replicates in which a method did not return finite estimates and intervals, the run time is the median time (in seconds) for a single fit.

one <- results[results$param == "beta", ]
do.call(rbind, lapply(split(one, one$method), function(d) {
    data.frame(method = d$method[1], replicates = nrow(d),
               failure_rate = round(mean(!d$ok), 3),
               median_seconds = round(median(d$time), 2))
})) |>
    knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)


ggplot(one, aes(x = method, y = time, fill = method)) +
    geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_y_log10() + xlab("") + ylab("seconds per fit (log scale)") +
    theme_classic()



6.5.2 Estimates
The boxplots show the distribution of the estimates over the replicates for each method, the dashed line is the true value. A method that recovers the parameter well is centred on the line (low bias) with a narrow box (low variability). The intercept is usually well estimated, while the range and the standard deviation of the field are typically much harder to estimate, in particular in a small domain with a few hundred events, so more spread for these two is not surprising.

ggplot(good, aes(x = method, y = est, fill = method)) +
    geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth), linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~ param, scales = "free_y", nrow = 1) +
    xlab("") + ylab("estimate") +
    theme_classic() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))



6.5.3 Bias, RMSE, and interval width
The table gives, for each method and parameter, the mean bias (estimate minus truth), the relative bias (bias as a proportion of the truth), the RMSE and the mean width of the 95% intervals. Bias and RMSE are averaged over the replicates where the fit succeeded.

summ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(good, list(good$method, good$param), drop = TRUE),
                              function(d) {
    data.frame(method = d$method[1], param = d$param[1], n = nrow(d),
               bias = mean(d$error), rel_bias = mean(d$error) / d$truth[1],
               rmse = sqrt(mean(d$error^2)),
               width = mean(d$upper - d$lower),
               coverage = mean(d$covered))
}))
summ <- summ[order(summ$param, summ$method), ]
knitr::kable(summ[, c("param", "method", "n", "bias", "rel_bias", "rmse", "width")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

Things to look for: (1) does the bias differ between stelfi and inlabru, and does the bias in the range and standard deviation change in size between the empirical Bayes and the default inlabru (the latter integrates over the hyperparameters and tends to give larger posterior means for scale parameters when the likelihood is skewed)? (2) is the RMSE dominated by bias or by variability? If the RMSE is close to the standard deviation of the estimates the error is mostly variability, while if it is much bigger the method is systematically off. (3) the priors in inlabru pull estimates, a lower RMSE for the range or standard deviation could be due to the prior, and might be a feature of the particular prior chosen here, see Section 6.6.


6.5.4 Coverage
Finally, the proportion of replicates in which the 95% interval contained the true value is plotted, with a band of \(\pm 1.96\) Monte Carlo standard errors. Coverage well below 95% means intervals are too narrow and the uncertainty is understated, coverage well above 95% means they are conservative (too wide). Remember that the stelfi intervals are Wald intervals based on the Laplace approximation, and the inlabru intervals are credible intervals, and that the eb version of inlabru ignores the uncertainty in the hyperparameters when calculating the uncertainty for the intercept.

summ$mc_se <- sqrt(summ$coverage * (1 - summ$coverage) / summ$n)
ggplot(summ, aes(x = method, y = coverage, colour = method)) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = coverage - 1.96 * mc_se, ymax = coverage + 1.96 * mc_se),
                    show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_wrap(~ param, nrow = 1) +
    ylim(0, 1) + xlab("") + ylab("coverage of 95% interval") +
    theme_classic() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))

title: 6  Parameter recovery: stelfi vs inlabru
text:
6.6 Extending the study
The set-up above is a single scenario. The same code can be used to explore how the conclusions change by altering:

the mesh: change mesh_fit to a coarser or finer mesh (as in Section 5.5.5) to see how bias in the range and standard deviation changes, and how the run times of the two packages scale with the number of nodes.
the number of events: change true_beta. Fewer events carry less information about the field, so bias and interval widths for the range and the standard deviation are expected to grow.
the strength of the spatial signal: change true_sigma and true_range.
the priors in inlabru: change prior.range and prior.sigma (e.g., a much weaker prior, or a prior centred on the truth) to see how much of the inlabru result is due to the prior rather than to the data. Note that stelfi has no priors.
the starting values for stelfi: starting further from the truth shows how often the optimiser fails, which is relevant given the warnings elsewhere in this book that some models are sensitive to starting values.
the domain: replacing the disc with a more complicated region (as in Section 5.5).





Bachl, Fabian E., Finn Lindgren, David L. Borchers, and Janine B. Illian. 2019. “inlabru: An R Package for Bayesian Spatial Modelling from Ecological Survey Data.” Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10: 760–66. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13168.

title: 7  Spatiotemporal LGCP
text:
7.1 An applied example: terrorism events in Iraq by year
The LGCP model can also be used for spatiotemporal modelling where there is autoregressive temporal dependence.
To achieve this, we choose an arbitrary number of time knots. The equation for an AR(1) process is as follows: \[\Lambda_i(s) = \text{exp}(\beta_0 + G_i(s) + \epsilon)\] where \(i\) indexes the time knot. \(\Lambda_i(s)\) is the field intensity at time knot \(i\), and \(G_i(s)\) the GMRF at the same time knot. Each \(G_i(s)\) shares common values for \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\).
Successive random fields are correlated through the formula \[G_i(s)=\rho G_{i-1}(s) + \epsilon_i\] where \(\rho\) is a constant between -1 and +1, and \(\epsilon_i\) is normally distributed with mean 0.
The iraq_terrorism data (see Section 5.5 for the spatial-only analysis) also record the year of each event, so the intensity can be allowed to change from year to year. Here one time knot per year is used, so \(G_i(s)\) is the field in year \(i\) and \(\rho\) describes how strongly one year’s spatial pattern carries over into the next.

title: 7  Spatiotemporal LGCP
text:
Warning



This example is a work in progress. The code has not yet been confirmed to run to completion with the current version of stelfi, so the chunks are not evaluated (eval: false). The model is sensitive to the starting values and to the time mesh, see the notes below.



7.1.1 Preparing the data
The spatial preparation is exactly as in Section 5.5 (project to UTM zone 38N, convert to km, and obtain the boundary of Iraq), but is repeated here so that this chapter can be run on its own. The only addition is the time of each event. Years are shifted so that the first year is \(t = 0\) and the time axis is then in years.

require(sf)
data("iraq_terrorism", package = "stelfi")
iraq_coordinates <- sf::st_coordinates(iraq_terrorism) |> as.data.frame()
names(iraq_coordinates) <- c("Longitude", "Latitude")
points_utm <- sf::st_as_sf(iraq_coordinates, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638)
locs_km <- as.data.frame(sf::st_coordinates(points_utm) / 1000)
names(locs_km) <- c("x", "y")
## time of each event, in years since the first year of data
year <- as.numeric(iraq_terrorism$iyear)
locs_km$t <- year - min(year)
range(locs_km$t)

iraq_sf <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(country = "Iraq", scale = "medium",
                                       returnclass = "sf") |>
    sf::st_transform(crs = 32638) |>
    sf::st_union() |>
    sf::st_make_valid()
iraq_sf_km <- sf::st_sf(geometry = sf::st_geometry(iraq_sf) / 1000)
sf::st_crs(iraq_sf_km) <- NA



7.1.2 Space and time meshes
A spatiotemporal model has a GMRF at every time knot, so the cost is roughly the number of spatial nodes multiplied by the number of time knots. A coarser spatial mesh than in the purely spatial example is therefore used (see Section 5.1).
The time mesh has one knot per year. It is extended one knot beyond the last year of data so that the events in the final year do not sit on the very edge of the time mesh.

smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(loc = locs_km[, 1:2],
                             boundary = fmesher::fm_as_segm(iraq_sf_km),
                             max.edge = c(100, 400), cutoff = 20)
smesh$n
## knots at 0, 1, ..., (last year + 1)
tmesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_1d(0:(max(locs_km$t) + 1))
tmesh$loc







Note



The time knots must be on the same scale as the t column of locs. A common mistake is to give the knots only as the two end points, e.g., seq(0, 5, by = 5), which gives just two knots (0 and 5) and so a single “step” over the whole period rather than one field per year. Check tmesh$loc to see the knots that were actually created.




7.1.3 Fitting the model
Starting values are important. For the intercept the average number of events per km\(^2\) per time unit is a sensible place to start (the log intensity of a surface that is flat over both space and time). For the range of the field, which is \(\sqrt{8}/\kappa\), a starting value of 300 km is chosen, and \(\tau\) is started at a small value.

n_years <- max(locs_km$t) + 1
area_km2 <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(iraq_sf_km))
start <- c(beta = log(nrow(locs_km) / (area_km2 * n_years)),
           log_tau = log(0.1),
           log_kappa = log(sqrt(8) / 300),
           atanh_rho = 0.2)
fit <- fit_lgcp(locs = locs_km, sf = iraq_sf_km, smesh = smesh, tmesh = tmesh,
                parameters = start)
get_coefs(fit)

The coefficients are the same as the spatial model, with an additional parameter \(\rho\) (reported on the atanh scale, so \(\rho = \text{tanh}(\text{atanh\_rho})\)) that is the correlation between the fields of consecutive years. A value of \(\rho\) close to 1 means the spatial pattern of events is very persistent from year to year, whereas a value near 0 means each year’s pattern is almost unrelated to the previous one.


7.1.4 Plotting the intensity over time
The estimated intensity at a particular time knot is plotted using show_lambda() and the timestamp argument as above (the index of the time knot). Here the first and the last year of data are shown.

show_lambda(fit, smesh = smesh, sf = iraq_sf_km, tmesh = tmesh,
            timestamp = 1, clip = TRUE) +
    ggplot2::theme_void() + ggplot2::ggtitle(paste("Year", min(year)))
show_lambda(fit, smesh = smesh, sf = iraq_sf_km, tmesh = tmesh,
            timestamp = n_years, clip = TRUE) +
    ggplot2::theme_void() + ggplot2::ggtitle(paste("Year", max(year)))

If the fit does not converge, things to try are: a coarser spatial mesh, different starting values (in particular beta, log_tau, and atanh_rho), or fitting each year as a separate spatial LGCP (Chapter 5) first to get an idea of reasonable values for \(\beta_0\), \(\tau\), and \(\kappa\).

title: 8  Spatiotemporal self-exciting models
text:
8.1 Fitting a spatiotemporal Hawkes process
For the spatiotemporal Hawkes processes fitted by stelfi, temporal self-excitement follows an exponential decay function (see Reinhart (2018)). The self-excitement over space follows a Gaussian distribution centered at the triggering event. The default is that the Gaussian function has a fixed covariance matrix, independent of time. Alternatively, covariance can be directly proportional to time, meaning that the self-excitement radiates out from the center over time. This can be appropriate when the mechanism causing self-excitement travels at a finite speed, but is very memory-intensive.
The intensity function used by stelfi is
\[\lambda(s,t) = \mu + \alpha \Sigma_{i:\tau_i<t}(\text{exp}(-\beta * (t-\tau_i)) G_i(s-x_i, t - \tau_i)).\]
Here \(\mu\) is the background rate, \(\beta\) is the rate of temporal decay, \(\alpha\) is the increase in intensity after an event, \(\tau_i\) are the event times, \(x_i\) are the event locations (in 2D Euclidean space) and \(G_i(s-x_i, t - \tau_i)\) is the spatial self-excitement kernel.
For the version with time-independent spatial excitement: \(G_i(s-x_i, t - \tau_i) = f_X(s - x_i)\) where \(f_X\) is the density function of \(X \sim \text{N}(0, \Sigma)\), (\(\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_x^2 & \rho  \\ \rho  & \sigma_y^2  \end{pmatrix}\)).
For the version with time-dependent spatial excitement: \(G_i(s-x_i, t - \tau_i) = f_X(s - x_i)\) where \(f_X\) is the density function of \(X \sim \text{N}(0, (t-\tau_i)\Sigma)\)
data(xyt, package = "stelfi")
locs <- data.frame(x = xyt$x, y = xyt$y)
times <- xyt$t
domain <- sf::st_as_sf(xyt$window)
ggplot(data = locs, aes(x = x, y = y, size = times)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_sf(data = domain, fill = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    theme_void()
bnd <- fmesher::fm_as_segm(as.matrix(sf::st_coordinates(domain)[, 1:2]))
smesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d(boundary = bnd, 
                            max.edge = 0.75, cutoff = 0.3)
param <- list(mu = 1, alpha = 3, beta = 6, xsigma = 0.2,
             ysigma = 0.2, rho = 0)
fit <- fit_stelfi(times = times, locs = locs, sf = domain, smesh = smesh, parameters = param)
pars <- get_coefs(fit)
Note that the coefs estimates are the vector of coefficients (on the log scale) of any supplied covariates, the first element related to the intercept (here the log of \(\mu\)). The estimate temporal self-excitement (ignoring and spatial influence) can be shown using show_hawkes() as in Chapter 2.
show_hawkes(list(times = times, params = c(mu = pars[1, 1], alpha = pars[3,1], beta = pars[4, 1])))
The bivariate Gaussian component of the diffusion kernel
## bivariate Gaussian kernel
sigma_x <- pars[5,1]
sigma_y <- pars[6,1]
rho <- pars[7,1]
x <- y <- seq(-2, 2, 0.1)
sigma <- matrix(c(sigma_x, rho, rho, sigma_y), 
                 ncol = 2)
f <- function(x, y) mvtnorm::dmvnorm(cbind(x, y), c(0,0), sigma)
z <- outer(x,y,f)
contour(x, y, z, nlevels = 10,  asp = 1)
